ARTICLE IN PRESS Applying the fuzzy distinction method to analyze the precautionary area of the wind farm along the western coast of Taiwan S Abstract S E In recent years, Taiwan has undertaken significantR efforts to establish and develop Offshore P Wind Farms (OWFs) in its western coastal region. Previous studies on Precautionary Area (PA) planning have predominantly focused on ship tNraffic density, and while ignoring marine environ- I ment protection issues, revealing a gap in comprehensive analysis. Therefore, the study examines E Taiwan's western Offshore Wind Farm (OWF) area and develops a Precautionary Area (PA) plan- L ning model. The new PA concept cConsiders not only navigational safety but also ecological sensi- I tivity, as well as wind and hydrological factors. This approach aims to harmonize different marine T activities, ensuring sustainRable and efficient development of Taiwan's green energy sector. Firstly, A this study collected ship navigation data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS). Secondly, the AIS data are processed and analyzed through a Marine Geographic Information System (MGIS) for a detailed spatial analysis of the marine environment. Thirdly, Fuzzy Logic Control (FLC) is used to manage marine data's inherent uncertainties and complexities, creating a more adaptable and nuanced model. By integrating AIS, MGIS, and FLC, the study develops an alternative PA planning model that enhances navigational and ecological safety while planning offshore wind farms. The alternative PA could facilitate the sustainable growth of Taiwan's green energy sector. Introduction With the intensification of the atmospheric crisis and the impacts of the first oil crisis, countries worldwide have realized the importance of energy diversification and security. The dras- tic fluctuations in oil prices have not only affected the cost of living for the general public but have also had a profound impact on industrial production, transportation, and global supply chains, thus affecting the global economy (Alpanda and Peralta-Alva 2010). To address the energy crisis, coun- tries worldwide have begun investing more in the development of renewable energy and nuclear energy to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, which has also driven a transformation in energy policies and technological innovation. When fossil fuels and nuclear energy fail to provide sus- S tainable and secure energy supplies, renewable energy has begun to gain more attention. Common S types of renewable energy include solar energy, wind energy, hydroelectric energy, biomass energy, E geothermal energy, and marine energy (Ang et al. 2022R). Among these, wind power has gained support and investment from governments worldwideP due to its enormous development potential. According to the statistical data from the GlobNal Wind Energy Council (2024), as of 2023, the I global offshore wind power capacity has reached 75.2 GW (Gigawatts), with 10.8 GW of new E capacity added that year. Taiwan accounts for 6% of the total capacity. L C Taiwan is an island nation surrounded by the sea and located in a subtropical monsoon I region, offering stable and aTbundant wind resources. The weather conditions provide a unique R advantage for the development of wind power. However, wind turbines are often considered un- A desirable facilities due to the limited land areas and proximity to densely populated areas. Building wind turbines offshore not only offers a larger area compared to land but also helps avoid issues like noise pollution that may affect nearby residents. Therefore, offshore wind power development has become a key focus of Taiwan's renewable energy strategy (Yue et al. 2019). Offshore wind power can provide clean, pollution-free electricity and reduce Taiwan's dependence on imported energy. In recent years, Taiwan has actively developed offshore wind farms (OWFs) through vari- ous strategies and incentives, including attracting direct investment, announcing candidate sites for OWFs, and leading large-scale development. Currently, Taiwan has established several opera- tive offshore wind farms (OWFs) around the western coast of Taiwan, including Formosa I, For- mosa II, Taiwan Power Company Offshore Wind Farm Phase I, Changfang & Xidao, Greater ARTICLE IN PRESS Changhua I, and Greater Changhua II. Recently, navigation safety and navigation risk assessment in offshore wind farms have been critical and a hot issue. Therefore, Taiwan actively develops intelligent navigation safety plans for western Taiwan wind farms by utilizing marine GIS (MGIS). For navigation safety, the spatial supporting platform has been employed in the Vessel Traffic Service (VTS) for the Taiwan channel monitoring mission by using MGIS. Additionally, Taiwan is actively developing a 4D smart port management system using the 4D metaverse technology. However, the development of offshore wind farms (OWFs) inevitably faces resource com- petition and may encroach on the rights of other maritime users (Tsai et al. 2022), such as fishing S boats and commercial vessels. In light of this, planning appropriate shipping channels and precau- S tionary areas (PA) is critical. E R The area within the proposed OWF sites in wPestern Taiwan includes many fishing ports along the western coastline. The construction oNf OWFs will compress the fishing areas tradition- ally used by fishermen, potentially posing a riIsk of accidents to fishing vessels. Furthermore, when commercial vessels navigate near wind fEarms or enter planned shipping channels and PA, there is L a potential risk of collisions that could damage the vessel's hull or wind turbine structures, leading C to oil or chemical spills and causIing environmental pollution, as well as the potential for casualties. T Therefore, it is important to give significant attention to vessel collisions with wind turbines (Mou- R las et al. 2017). A Shipping channels and PA are crucial safety measures, particularly in areas with complex traffic flow and higher collision risks (Li et al. 2015). The authorities typically plan PAs in high- risk maritime areas, and vessels must wait outside the area for confirmation from relevant maritime authorities before entering. Additionally, vessels are required to exercise heightened caution while navigating within these areas (International Maritime Organization 1985). The function of a PA is similar to a traffic intersection on land, often located where multiple shipping channels or roads converge (Figure 1). Traffic flow in these areas comes from various directions, making collisions or other safety incidents highly likely (Pietrzykowski and Magaj 2017). Strengthening the man- agement and rational planning of PAs can effectively improve traffic safety levels and significantly reduce accident probabilities to ensure the safety of all vessels and related maritime facilities ARTICLE IN PRESS within the areas. << Insert Figure 1 here>> Figure 1. Automatic Identification System An Automatic Identification System (AIS) is a technology used for communication and positioning between vessels and between vessels and shore-based stations. It was initially designed to improve navigation safety and is now used for monitoring vessel traffic, managing harbor traffic ARTICLE IN PRESS flow, and executing maritime safety-related tasks. AIS operates in accordance with regulations established by organizations such as the International Maritime Organization and the International Association of Marine Aids to Navigation and Lighthouse Authorities. In addition, the Interna- tional Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), which came into force in 2000, specifies in Chapter V, Regulation 19, that vessels with 300 gross tonnage or greater on international routes, vessels with 500 gross tonnage or greater on non-international routes, and all passenger vessels must equipped AIS, which must remain operational at all times. This regulation mainly covers the following items (International Maritime Organization 2002): (1) Provide information: Vessel identity, type, position, speed, navigation status, and other safety-related information. (2) Automatically receive information from other vessels. S (3) Monitor and track vessels. S (4) Exchange data with shore-based stations. E R AIS integrates technologies such as the Global Positioning System (GPS) and Very High P Frequency (VHF) radio, using two channels in the VHF range—87B (161.975 MHz) and 88B N (162.025 MHz)—for data transmission and reception. AIS shipborne equipment is classified into I Class A and Class B. Vessels regulated by the SOLAS convention are required to be equipped E with Class A devices. Marine Geographic Information System A Geographic Information System (GIS) combines software, hardware, data, and analytical tools to allow users to visualize and understand various geographical phenomena and the spatial relationships of different types of spatial data. A basic GIS includes spatial data, attribute data, coordinate systems, and layers. Spatial data can be divided into two main types: vector data, which ARTICLE IN PRESS consists of points, lines, and polygons, and raster data, which consists of grids. These are overlaid in multiple layers for computational and analytical purposes. In recent years, scholars have applied GIS data, concepts, and tools in the marine field, resulting in the development of the Marine Geo- graphic Information System (MGIS). Fuzzy Theory Zadeh (1965) proposed the original fuzzy theory. Its core concept is the fuzzy sets, which differs from traditional sets based on binary logic that only have two extreme values — “belong” or “do not belong”—without any gray areas. However, in reality, human thinking logic is not lim- ited to just 0 or 1. For example, there is no specific boundary for the degree of temperature; using binary logic would not provide practical information. Fuzzy sets use membership functions to cre- ate a range between 0 and 1 and represent the degree to which a value belongs to the set with a membership degree. The closer the degree is to 1, the higher the membership degree. Fuzzy sets align more closely with human thinking patterns and natural langSuage, offering greater flexibility S in handling complex real-life problems. In recent years, the fuzzy theory has been applied to vari- E ous fields, particularly in decision-making and renewable energy evaluation (Du et al. 2022; R Hussain, Ullah, Senapati et al. 2024; Hussain, Yin, UPllah et al. 2024; Zeb et al. 2024). N Figure 4 shows the basic structure of Fuzzy Logic Control (FLC), which includes Fuzzifier, I Fuzzy Rule Base, Fuzzy Inference Engine, and Defuzzifier. First, the fuzzifier converts precise E input data into fuzzy numbers, where membership functions are used to map the input data to fuzzy L C sets with fuzzy meanings. This study fuzzified the initial precise data to triangular fuzzy numbers. I The fuzzy rule base is createdT using multiple fuzzy rules based on IF-THEN statements. The rules are generally formulated bRased on expert experience or historical data, and the membership degree A of the input data is calculated to determine which rules are triggered. The fuzzy inference engine simulates human thinking and decision-making patterns, performing reasoning with the fuzzy rule base and computing the fuzzy output. << Insert Figure 4 here>> Figure 4. Finally, the fuzzy output values are transformed into clear and actionable output values in defuzzification. The Center of Gravity method is the most commonly used defuzzification technique. The final output value is obtained by calculating the centroid of the output function. This architecture helps simplify the overall system design, effectively lower R the computational loadA, and reduce the complexity of the rule base. Based on this approach, the outputs of the sub-models are progressively combined into the final stage model, ultimately producing a comprehensive decision result, which makes the overall fuzzy model more flexible and adaptable (Balmat et al. 2011). 3. Fuzzy Logic Control Model for Precautionary Area The Fuzzy Logic Control (FLC) model in this study consists of three phases and seven fuzzy sub-models (Figure 5). Each fuzzy sub-model has two inputs and one output, where the ARTICLE IN PRESS output values serve as inputs for the next stage, utilizing triangular fuzzy numbers for calculation. This model aims to analyze the factors affecting the precautionary area planning and then decide the optimal PA. The first phase comprises four sub-models (aspects): Wind Factors (wind speed and wind direction), Hydrological Factors (ocean depth and ocean currents), Ecological Sensitivity (protected areas and fisheries), and Navigational Safety (traffic density and distance to OWF). The second phase involves the Environmental Index (comprising Wind Factors and Hydrological Fac- tors) and the Safety Index (encompassing Ecological Sensitivity and Navigational Safety). Finally, the third phase uses the Environmental Index and Safety Index as inputs, with the output being the PA indicator value. Environmental Index (EI) and Safety Index (SI) R When vessels Anavigate at sea, their track, stability, and speed are inevitably affected by various factors, such as sea states and environmental conditions. Strong winds and currents in- crease the torque exerted on the vessel, which can cause deviations from the planned route (Chen et al. 2015). The impact of water depth on vessel navigation is also significant. In deep waters, the distance between the vessel’s hull and the seabed is greater, reducing the resistance encountered by the vessel. In shallow waters, however, the vessel’s resistance increases substantially due to the shallow water effect, causing the vessel to pitch more severely and potentially leading to phenom- ena such as squatting, which could result in the vessel sinking or the bow rising, thereby affecting navigation stability (Zhen et al. 2023). Discussion Although Taiwan has completed several offshore farms along its western coast, it has not yet fully completed all offshore wind farms. That is, Taiwan will build more offshore wind farms in the future. The analysis approach and the FLC model would be applied to other offshore wind farms to analyze the navigational risk. It is the operational management implications. One of the challenges is that the AIS data used in this study is historic data rather than real- time data. To increase the efficiency of the analysis method, future studies could utilize real-time data to analyze real-time environmental conditions, providing real-time navigational risks. Some typhoons visit the Taiwanese coasts every year. The typhoons not only cause damage S to offshore wind turbines but also disrupt the navigational safety of vessels in the waters of offshore S wind farms around the western coast of Taiwan. Conclusion L In recent years, Taiwan haCs actively promoted the development of OWF in the western coast. However, the planning prIocess needs to balance multiple dimensions, including shipping, T fisheries, and ecological cRonservation. This study aims to apply scientific methods to plan wind A farm shipping channels and PA, ensuring the smooth advancement and sustainable development of offshore wind power. Previous PA planning primarily considered vessel traffic density. However, this study in- corporates sustainable development technologies as one of the factors, combining them with vessel traffic density to propose an alternative PA plan that considers multiple factors. This plan ensures both navigational safety and ecological conservation during the development and future use of OWFs, while also considering wind and hydrological factors. This study first integrates AIS historical data with MGIS and maps the vessel traffic density distribution in the western OWF area of Taiwan. The vessel density is higher around Taichung and Mailiao harbors, with vessels primarily concentrated along the northward shipping channel on the ARTICLE IN PRESS eastern side of the Changhua Wind Farm channel. Furthermore, some areas of the future third- phase wind farm still overlap with existing vessel traffic tracks, and future adjustments to shipping channels and PA will be required to balance wind farm and shipping demands. To mitigate the impact of particular variables or factors on the ultimate calculation results, the FLC model in this paper treats all unprocessed information as equally important in its initial phase without additional weights, and then calculates the PA indicator value. Additionally, this study employs min-max normalization to adjust the fuzzy output results and linearly scale the scores between 0 and 10 according to the original data distribution. Finally, the results are pre- sented in numerical and color scale formats overlaid on nautical charts in MGIS. The study results S show that high-score areas in the precautionary area primarily concentrate in the northern region, S as well as in the southwestern waters alongside the Changhua wind farm shipping channel. Com- E pared with the original precautionary area, the proposedR plan requires an extension of 2 to 6 nau- P tical miles towards the north, focusing on managing the areas alongside the Changhua wind farm shipping channel, ensuring that the new precautNionary area adapts to the development of Taiwan's I OWF industry. E In the future, ships must strictlLy comply with relevant regulations, and maritime authorities C and other industries operating in the sea areas must engage in complete and thorough communica- I tion and coordination. This coTllaborative effort will help build a safe maritime traffic network and R promote the symbiotic development of the green energy industry, shipping safety, and the ecolog- A ical environment in the OWF. The proposed FLC model for PA planning in this study can be adapted for use in other ports or offshore wind farms worldwide by modifying data and parameters, such as traffic density, eco- logical environment, and hydrological conditions. This study contributes to academics and practice. Furthermore, artificial intelligence (AI) is a powerful tool and decision-making methodology that has been applied to various fields (Kao et al. 2020; Senapati et al. 2024; Senapati et al. 2025). Therefore, future studies could combine FLC and AI to solve the PA problems more efficiently. JSON: Name: fuzzy_pa_planning Title: A multi-layer Mamdani fuzzy-logic pipeline integrating AIS and MGIS for precautionary-area delineation around offshore wind farms Short Hypothesis: A multi-layer Mamdani fuzzy logic model that integrates AIS-derived traffic density, ecological sensitivity, wind, and hydrological factors will produce PA delineations with lower predicted collision risk (as measured by an encounter-based collision probability model) than PA delineations produced by traffic-density-only and conventional probabilistic risk-assessment baselines. Related Work: Existing approaches for PA planning and navigational risk assessment fall into three broad classes: (1) traffic-density or kernel-density based zoning using AIS to identify high-use corridors; (2) probabilistic and accident-record-driven risk assessments that estimate collision probabilities from historical incidents and stochastic models; and (3) multi-criteria and fuzzy-based frameworks (including fuzzy-Delphi, MCDM, and evidential-reasoning extensions) that aggregate qualitative and quantitative attributes. Limitations across these approaches include: heavy reliance on traffic density alone which ignores ecological and environmental constraints; probabilistic methods that underperform when incident records are sparse or non-stationary; MCDM techniques that require explicit weighting and can be brittle under uncertainty; and fuzzy/Delphi variants that may overestimate risk due to subjective rule elicitation and do not always integrate spatial MGIS layers or handle large rule-bases efficiently. Few existing methods jointly integrate AIS, high-resolution spatial layers (bathymetry, currents, wind, protected areas, fisheries), and a computationally tractable fuzzy inference architecture validated against encounter-model metrics. Abstract: This project develops a structured research pipeline that applies a multi-layer Mamdani fuzzy-logic control model to delineate precautionary areas (PAs) around offshore wind farms by integrating AIS traffic, marine GIS layers, wind and hydrodynamic data, and ecological sensitivity indicators. The pipeline constructs a 2-step spatial preprocessing stage (grid-based AIS kernel density and thematic MGIS layers) and a three-phase fuzzy model: low-level sub-models for wind, hydrology, ecology, and navigational safety; mid-level environmental and safety indices; and a final PA index with centroid defuzzification. The primary contribution is a reproducible experimental framework to compare PA outputs against traffic-density-only and probabilistic baselines using encounter-based collision-probability metrics and historical incident records where available. Expected outcomes are spatially explicit PA delineations that better reflect multi-objective maritime safety and conservation priorities and objectively lower predicted collision risk in validation tests, while exposing sensitivity to membership functions and input coverage. The pipeline is designed for transfer to other ports and OWF sites. Experiments: Datasets: (1) AIS dataset: continuous vessel position records from shore-based and satellite AIS covering the target OWF region for 12 months (timestamped MMSI, lat/lon, heading, speed, vessel type); (2) MGIS layers: nautical charts, OWF polygons, Traffic Separation Schemes, bathymetry grid, modeled ocean currents (monthly/seasonal), wind fields (hourly), ecological protected-area polygons, fisheries activity KDE from gear-specific logs; (3) incident log: historical near-miss and collision reports for the region (if available) or synthetic encounter labels derived from high-fidelity encounter simulator. Baselines: (A) KDE-traffic-only PA (thresholded density); (B) probabilistic collision-risk model calibrated on AIS encounters; (C) weighted-sum MCDM using same input layers; (D) fuzzy-Delphi/FTA model variant. Evaluation metrics: area under ROC for predicting historical incidents, precision/recall at grid-cell level, mean predicted collision probability over vessel tracks, false-positive area ratio (area flagged / total study area), spatial Jaccard similarity to regulatory PA, computational runtime, and sensitivity-to-input-noise (RMSE of PA index under perturbed AIS). Experimental setup: discretize study region into 2-nautical-mile cells; compute per-cell input features (traffic KDE, mean wind speed/direction, current magnitude, depth, distance-to-protected-area, fishery density); implement multi-layer Mamdani FLC with triangular membership functions and centroid defuzzification; perform temporal cross-validation (leave-one-month-out) and report aggregated metrics with 95% confidence intervals. Ablation studies: (1) remove ecological inputs; (2) remove hydrological inputs; (3) replace Mamdani inference with Sugeno; (4) single-layer vs multi-layer fuzzy architecture; (5) alternative defuzzification (COG vs bisector); (6) compare with and without Min-Max normalization of outputs. Statistical tests: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests between primary pipeline and each baseline for collision-probability and ROC metrics (alpha=0.05). Implementation notes: data preprocessing and KDE in Python (GeoPandas, scikit-learn), MGIS visualization in ArcGIS/Pro, fuzzy models in MATLAB or Python fuzzy libraries; run-time profiling on a workstation with 16 CPU cores and 64 GB RAM. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sparse or biased AIS coverage (small fishing vessels or transient craft without AIS) can underrepresent traffic and distort KDE inputs; ecological and fisheries data may be temporally misaligned with AIS leading to mismatched feature snapshots; membership functions and rule base elicitation are subjective and can produce divergent outputs across experts; multi-layer fuzzy systems scale poorly if number of inputs increases, leading to rule explosion or oversmoothing of outputs; normalization and defuzzification choices can compress dynamic range and obscure spatial contrasts; lack of reliable historical incident labels limits direct validation and may force reliance on simulated encounters; transferability to other regions is constrained by differing traffic compositions, regulatory regimes, and data availability; computational cost grows with finer grid resolution and with real-time streaming AIS requirements; policy or regulatory acceptance of fuzzy-derived PAs may be limited without demonstrable empirical incident reduction.
